answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and only one decision this cycle. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2 is explicit that the low-cost vendor missed SLA in 3 of 4 quarters and must not be sole source on a critical line — exactly the trap the 18% mandate creates), rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback applied to a NON-critical renewal; this contract does not auto-renew and the line has no buffer, so lapse risk is real), and deprioritizes add_second_source (memory_c3 is valuable but dual-sourcing takes qualification time it cannot deliver inside 14 days, and it adds cost rather than cutting 18%). Straight renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects delivery but banks zero of the mandated savings. Negotiating at renewal is the only path that touches cost and delivery risk simultaneously: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says a longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope — combined, that is the plausible route to a large share of 18% while keeping the integration and delivery schedule intact. I verify c4 and c6 because my entire plan rests on their magnitude and comparability: I need the original records to see whether the savings were anywhere near 18% and whether they came from this component class at this volume, or from a small non-critical spend that will not generalize. I did not verify c2 because its cautionary content only strengthens the decision if true and its failure mode is unacceptable regardless. Uncertainty retained: each memory is a single archived instance with no counterfactual; if verification shows c4/c6 savings were marginal or from an unlike category, the 18% target likely cannot be met by negotiation alone and the honest move is to book the achievable savings, refuse to close the gap by degrading supply reliability, and escalate the shortfall to finance rather than absorb it as delivery risk. Downstream risk flagged: a hard cost mandate plus a memory stating 'low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply' invites a future session to read the archive as endorsement of switching and drop the SLA caveat; I want the multi-year term written with benchmark reopeners and an explicit note that the 94%-utilization/no-buffer condition, not vendor loyalty, is what excluded the cheaper vendor. Scale is a standard negotiation rather than a broad restructuring: single contract, service scope held constant, second-sourcing queued as the next review's decision so the memory_c3 single-point-of-failure lesson is not lost, only deferred.
